Steady states

Source: vignettes/articles/methods-steady-states.Rmd
methods-steady-states.Rmd

A model at rest before a stimulus starts from a root of the right-hand side. Pimpl() computes it numerically, steadyStates() in closed form. Guide: Setting up models.

Conserved quantities

With compartment volumes \(V_i\), stoichiometric coefficients \(S_{ri}\) of species \(i\) in reaction \(r\), and rates \(v_r\) in a frame of volume \(V_{f(r)}\), the right-hand side is

\[\dot x_i = f_i(x, p) = \frac{1}{V_i} \sum_r S_{ri}\, V_{f(r)}\, v_r(x, p). \tag{1}\]

Every \(w\) with \(S w = 0\) conserves the amount

\[\sum_i w_i V_i x_i \tag{2}\]

by (1); conservedQuantities() lists these amounts. Then \(f(x, p) = 0\) does not determine \(x\): every conservation class, the states with given totals, has separate roots.

Pseudo-transient continuation

Pimpl() adds the conservation laws \(C(p)\, x = T\), totals \(T\) as parameters:

\[G(x, p) = \begin{pmatrix} f(x, p) \\ C(p)\, x - T \end{pmatrix} = 0 . \tag{3}\]

Pseudo-transient continuation solves (3) by implicit Euler steps of \(\dot x = f(x, p)\) on the conservation manifold, with a pseudo-time step that grows as the residual falls. It follows the flow far from the root and becomes Newton’s method near it, so it reaches a stable steady state. A state no reaction changes keeps the given value. The solver is cppDE’s ptc(), called from C++ (step, convergence and stability tests).

Every root starts from the same guess, a function of parameters and controls, never from an earlier root, so the objective is the same function of the parameters in every call. Warm starts would change roots in the last digits, which the ODE step-size control magnifies in the objective.

Derivatives of the root

From \(G(x(p), p) = 0\) for all \(p\), the implicit function theorem gives

\[\frac{\partial G}{\partial x}\, \frac{\partial x}{\partial p} = -\frac{\partial G}{\partial p}, \tag{4}\]

regular where the steady state is isolated in the conservation class. Differentiating (4) again gives the second derivatives, Pimpl(deriv2 = TRUE), with the same matrix. A reverse sweep uses the transpose of (4) (Sensitivities and Hessians).

Stability

A root is a resting state only if every eigenvalue \(\lambda_k\) of \(J = \partial f / \partial x\) on the conservation manifold has negative real part. At a root whose leading eigenvalue has real part above stabilityTol, the solver continues along the leading eigenvector (cppDE); the evaluation fails if neither direction leads to a stable root. controlsPTC = list(stability = FALSE) returns the unstable root.

constraintStability() adds a term that rises towards the stability boundary:

\[w \sum_k r_k^2, \qquad r_k = \frac{\max\bigl(0,\ \mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_k - \lambda_0\bigr)}{\lambda_{tol} - \lambda_0}, \tag{5}\]

with \(\lambda_{tol}\) the stabilityTol of the Pimpl(), onset \(\lambda_0 = \lambda_{tol} - 1/T\) and \(T\) the time span of the data. The term is zero while every perturbation decays faster than the experiment lasts. Steady states that agree in all inputs count once. With right and left eigenvectors \(u_k\), \(w_k\) of \(J\) and (4),

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}\lambda_k}{\mathrm{d}\theta} = \frac{w_k^{\mathsf H} \bigl(\partial_\theta J + \partial_x J\, \mathrm{d}x^*/\mathrm{d}\theta\bigr) u_k} {w_k^{\mathsf H} u_k}, \tag{6} \]

which needs Pimpl(deriv2 = TRUE). The term is a model assumption, not data: profiles with stop = "data" and likelihood ratios leave it out.

At the onset, (5) and the gradient are continuous and the curvature jumps: below, term and Hessian are zero; above, the Gauss-Newton Hessian is

\[\frac{2 w}{(\lambda_{tol} - \lambda_0)^2} \sum_{k \,:\, \mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_k > \lambda_0} \frac{\mathrm{d}\,\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_k}{\mathrm{d}\theta} \frac{\mathrm{d}\,\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_k}{\mathrm{d}\theta}^{\mathsf T} , \tag{7}\]

nonzero as \(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_k \to \lambda_0\). A profile therefore takes small steps across the onset (Profile likelihood).

Analytical steady-state constraints

steadyStates() solves \(f(x, p) = 0\) in closed form [1], [2]. Each unknown, a state or a kinetic parameter, is solved from a combination of balances such that the solution is a ratio of sums of positive terms. The solution is thus positive for positive parameters, also with solveQuadratic = TRUE, which takes the positive root of a balance quadratic in the state. A state whose balance is spent on a kinetic parameter stays free, as the parameter of the steady-state value of the state. States that are zero in every steady state are set to 0. A conserved quantity keeps one state free. Volumes are never solved for.

The result, one equation per solved unknown, replaces identity entries of a parameter transformation:

steady <- steadyStates(reactions)
parameters <- getParameters(reactions)
trafo <- repar(eqnvec(setNames(parameters, parameters)), "x <- y",
               x = names(steady), y = steady)
p <- P(trafo)
argument effect
givenCQs conserved quantities, default from customTotals() or derived
neglect states and parameters never solved for
priority states solved first, parameters preferred as pivots
forcings states held at zero as exogenous inputs
solveQuadratic allow the positive root of a quadratic balance
file save the result with saveRDS()

Without a solution of this form, steadyStates() returns 0. The solver is a Python module (numpy, sympy, scipy) called through reticulate.

P() or Pexpl() evaluate the closed form explicitly with symbolic derivatives: no root search, no convergence failure, no solver tolerance in the objective, one parameter less per solved equation. Rosenblatt et al. report more reliable and faster optimization than with common numerical implementations [1]. steadyStates() does not test stability; Pimpl() does (Stability). Pimpl() is needed where no closed form of positive sums exists, as for the network of the guide.

Reference: conservedQuantities(), Pimpl(), steadyStates(), constraintStability()

References

[2]
D. Kaschek, W. Mader, M. Fehling-Kaschek, M. Rosenblatt, and J. Timmer, “dMod: Efficient parameter estimation and uncertainty analysis for dynamic models,” Journal of Statistical Software, vol. 88, no. 10, pp. 1–32, 2019, doi: 10.18637/jss.v088.i10.
